newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland toasts Clinton's presidential success.
newsitem.headline: Ireland toasts Clinton's presidential success.

text.p: Ireland toasted Bill Clinton's success at winning a second White House term with Guinness and hot dogs in the early hours of Wednesday morning in Dublin.
Ireland has strong links with its American cousins, often in the real sense, with about half its 80 million diaspora dotted throughout the United States.

"I am delighted that Clinton got in again. He is the only U.S. president, in my lifetime, who has shown a real interest in Ireland, not just the peace process but Ireland as a whole," one agricultural student from County Kerry in southern Ireland said.
"Bill's the man for Ireland," Cathy, a hotel manageress said waving a bottle of Budweiser beer in the air, "He has such a gentle smile I'd vote for him just for that alone."
She was speaking at a Dublin city centre bar which stayed open late to watch the U.S. election on television.

Clinton endeared himself to the Irish nation, receiving a "hundred thousand welcomes" the Irish greeting "cead mile failte", when he visited both the Republic of Ireland and the war-torn Northern Ireland a year ago this month.

He is expected to make a return visit to Ireland before Christmas to give a further push to a faltering peace process which was seriously jolted when the pro-nationalist Irish Republican Army guerrillas ended a 17-month ceasefire with a bomb blast in London early in 1996.

While most of Ireland slept throughout the election countdown those who were out partying were all well aware of who Clinton was and generally felt it was in the interests of Ireland that he was re-elected.
Few knew very much about opposition candidate Bob Dole.
"I think it is better that Clinton won for continuity of policy which Clinton embarked upon when he visited Dublin and Belfast," a Dublin solicitor said.

"He is a very powerful background presence to the peace process in Ireland. If somebody new got in, there would be discontinuity so I think this is good to assist that peace process and that is very important for Ireland."

During his election campaign, Clinton spoke of his wish to bring lasting peace to Northern Ireland and full-page advertisments appeared in Irish-American newspapers asking readers to turn out for Clinton in November.
